nodes.body:
1994 Jan 1. RGG; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution
note: There was no date on the original document so 1994 Jan 1 was assigned since most of the SLHs were prepared from 1994 thru 1997.

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Silverstripe halfbeak
Scientific Name: Hyporhamphus unifasciatus

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Atheriniformes
	Family:  Exocoetidae

Other Common Names: Halfbeak, ballyhoo, balao, Common Halfbeak; Atlantic Silverstripe Halfbeak


Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Ranzani 1842)
	Reference for Classification (Robins et al.1991)

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Sold as bait (Robins 1958).

Recreational:  Caught for bait by recreational fisherman, along relatives, ballyhoo, Hemiramphus brasiliensis and the balao, H. balao (McLane 1974; Manooch 1984).

Ecological Role:  This is an abundant omnivorous coastal and estuarine species which feeds on algae and seagrasses during the day, zooplankton at night (Gilmore 1972; Robertson and Howard 1978; Robertson and Klump 1983) and is subsequently consumed by various piscine predators (McLane 1974; Manooch 1984).  This species is considered a keystone nektonic species due to its numerical abundance and ubiquitous distribution in open estuarine waters.

Indicator:  None known.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Bays and estuaries from New Brunswick, Canada to Argentina including the Gulf of Mexico (Collette 1965; Leim and Scott 1966).  Indian River specimens may represent a distinct southern species which occurs from the mid-peninsula Florida to Argentina (Bruce Collette, personal communication).

Within Study Area: Occurs in seagrass meadows and along sandy beaches within the Indian River Lagoon (Gilmore 1972, 1977, 1985, 1988). Applied Biology).


Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Juveniles and adults usually diurnally and nocturnally active in schools or lose groups near surface waters over seagrass meadows and sand bottoms (Robertson and Howard 1978; Robertson and Klumpp 1983; Gilmore 1988).  Eggs are benthic in seagrass meadows (F. Douglas Martin in Hardy 1978), while larvae are apparently within the water column, though in shallow water, possibly seagrass meadows.
Movements and Migrations: Adults and juveniles make local migrations associated with seasonal changes in water temperature with a general inshore movement into warm temperate estuaries during the warmer months (Hildebrand and Schroeder 1928).  Exodus from estuaries during the winter (Whitewater Bay: Tabb and Manning 1961; Aransas Bay: Copeland 1965).  The only months Silverstripe halfbeaks were absent from the Indian River Lagoon seagrass collections were December and January, as adults (to 240 mm SL) were collected during all other months (Gilmore 1988; Gilmore unpubl. data).  The smallest individuals captured within the lagoon were 25 mm SL in March while specimens below 75 mm SL were captured March through July (Gilmore 1988; Gilmore unpub data).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type:  Eggs are benthic in seagrass meadows (F. Douglas Martin in Hardy 1978), while larvae are apparently within the water column, though in shallow water, possibly seagrass meadows. Juveniles and adults forage in groups near surface waters over seagrass meadows and adjacent to sandy beaches (Gilmore pers obs).  Often captured in surface waters at night (Hoese 1958).  Also occurs in tidal channels (Yarrow 1877) and along ocean and Gulf beaches, but is more typical of bay and estuarine waters.

Substrate:  Eggs are deposited on blades of seagrass (F. Douglas Martin in Hardy 1978).  Larvae are found principally in water column often in association with floating vegetation or debris (Gilmore pers. obs.).  Juveniles and adults occur principally in the water column and near the water's surface over sand and vegetated bottoms, such as seagrass meadows (Gilmore 1987, 1988; Robertson and Klumpp 1983; Breder and Rosen 1966).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body: The Silverstripe halfbeak is an euryhaline marine species which resides in estuaries within the southern portion of its range.  Northern ranging individuals (north of 28 00 N) typically spend a portion of their life history on the adjacent continental shelf (Gilmore 1972; Hardy 1978). Recorded from temperatures of 16.7-34.0 C, salinity 15.9-42.9 ppt (Roessler 1970).  Larva recorded from salinities of 0.00-12.0 ppt (Dovel 1971).  Juvenile and adult halfbeaks were present in the Indian River Lagoon seagrass meadows during all months except December and January at salinities of 17-38 ppt (25 ppt mean). Kilby (1954) has recorded the Silverstripe halfbeak from salinities as low as 7.5 ppt. in marshes of the Florida coast of the Gulf of Mexico.

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body: Reproductive Mode:  This species is gonochoristic, polygamous, oviparous, and iteroparous; eggs are fertilized externally (Hildebrand and Schroeder 1928; Breder and Rosen 1966; Hardy 1978).

nodes.title: Mating/Spawning
nodes.body:
Spawning apparently occurs over shallow seagrass meadows during the spring with 2.0 mm diameter egg deposition on grass blades (Hildebrand and Schroeder 1928; F. Douglas Martin in Hardy 1978).  Larvae are free swimming at 3.0 mm TL and have no beak though the dentary begins to elongate at 11 mm TL (Hildebrand and Schroeder 1928).  Young of the year are taken in most estuaries during the spring and summer (Hildebrand and Schroeder 1928; Kilby 1955; Reid 1954;  Springer and Woodburn 1960; Tabb and Manning 1961; Roessler 1970; Subrahmanyam and Drake 1975; Gilmore 1988).  Nothing is known of spawning behavior in this species although diurnal spawning in seagrass meadows with deposition of adhesive eggs on seagrass blades has been observed in Pacific species of Hyporhamphus (Hyporhamphus sajori [Temmink and Schlegal], Inaba 1931; Breder and Rosen 1966).

Fecundity: Nothing known.

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  Eggs are demersal, spherical, with chorionic bristles and filaments and 1.0 mm in diameter when ripe, 1.4 mm at ovulation, 2.0 mm when fertilized (Hildebrand and Schroeder 1928; Dovel 1971; Hardy and Johnson 1974; Hardy 1978).  Eggs have long adhesive chorionic filaments which allow attachment to vegetation (Hardy 1978).  The smallest free swimming larvae was 3.0 mm in length (Hildebrand and Schroeder 1928).

Larvae: Larvae range from 3.0 to 15.8 mm SL (Hardy and Johnson 1974).  Development rate unknown.

Juvenile:  Juveniles range from 22.5 to 140 mm SL (Hardy and Johnson 1974; Hardy 1978).  Developmental rate is unknown.  Juveniles school in pelagic waters over seagrass in estuaries during warm months (Hildebrand and Schroeder 1928; Kilby 1955; Reid 1954; Springer and Woodburn 1960; Tabb and Manning 1961; Roessler 1970; Subrahmanyam and Drake 1975; Gilmore 1988).

Adults:  Female maturation occurs at 147 mm SL (Beebe and Tee-Van 1928).  Age is unknown.

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: The feeding habits of larvae are unknown. Juveniles and adults omnivores feeding mostly on planktonic crustaceans and plant materials (algae and seagrass; Randall 1968; Gilmore 1972; Subrahmanyam and Drake 1975). Adults consume crabs, copepods, amphipods, polychaetes, and plant detritus (Gilmore 1972; Subrahmanyam and Drake 1975).  Estuarine halfbeaks of Australia (Hyporhamphus melanochir) switch from diurnal herbivory to nocturnal zooplankivory (Robertson and Howard 1978; Robertson and Klumpp 1983).  This may be true of the Silverstripe halfbeak as Gilmore (unpublished data) has observed plant detritus in guts of diurnally captured specimens, and a gut packed exclusively with copepods in nocturnal specimens from Santa Rosa Sound, Florida.

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Predation:  Due to its abundance in costal estuaries it is highly likely that the Silverstripe halfbeak plays an important role as prey for a variety of wetland predators.

Factors Influencing Populations:  There is some indication that Silverstripe halfbeaks depend on warm, relatively clear estuarine waters with seagrass meadows for reproduction and early development.  Therefore, loss of these water quality and seagrass decline which has taken place through much of the species range may have caused significant reductions in estuarine populations. Under natural conditions predation probably plays the most significant role in influencing population patterns.

sections.heading: HEADER
sections.content:
Title: Silverstripe halfbeak (Hyporhamphus unifasciatus)

FLELMR Code:  1368

sections.heading: Revisions
sections.content:
1994 Jan 1. RGG; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution
note: There was no date on the original document so 1994 Jan 1 was assigned since most of the SLHs were prepared from 1994 thru 1997.

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Common Name: Silverstripe halfbeak
Scientific Name: Hyporhamphus unifasciatus

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Atheriniformes
	Family:  Exocoetidae

Other Common Names: Halfbeak, ballyhoo, balao, Common Halfbeak; Atlantic Silverstripe Halfbeak


Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Ranzani 1842)
	Reference for Classification (Robins et al.1991)

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  Sold as bait (Robins 1958).

Recreational:  Caught for bait by recreational fisherman, along relatives, ballyhoo, Hemiramphus brasiliensis and the balao, H. balao (McLane 1974; Manooch 1984).

Ecological Role:  This is an abundant omnivorous coastal and estuarine species which feeds on algae and seagrasses during the day, zooplankton at night (Gilmore 1972; Robertson and Howard 1978; Robertson and Klump 1983) and is subsequently consumed by various piscine predators (McLane 1974; Manooch 1984).  This species is considered a keystone nektonic species due to its numerical abundance and ubiquitous distribution in open estuarine waters.

Indicator:  None known.

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  Bays and estuaries from New Brunswick, Canada to Argentina including the Gulf of Mexico (Collette 1965; Leim and Scott 1966).  Indian River specimens may represent a distinct southern species which occurs from the mid-peninsula Florida to Argentina (Bruce Collette, personal communication).

Within Study Area: Occurs in seagrass meadows and along sandy beaches within the Indian River Lagoon (Gilmore 1972, 1977, 1985, 1988). Applied Biology).


Mobility and Migration:

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content:
Juveniles and adults usually diurnally and nocturnally active in schools or lose groups near surface waters over seagrass meadows and sand bottoms (Robertson and Howard 1978; Robertson and Klumpp 1983; Gilmore 1988).  Eggs are benthic in seagrass meadows (F. Douglas Martin in Hardy 1978), while larvae are apparently within the water column, though in shallow water, possibly seagrass meadows.
Movements and Migrations: Adults and juveniles make local migrations associated with seasonal changes in water temperature with a general inshore movement into warm temperate estuaries during the warmer months (Hildebrand and Schroeder 1928).  Exodus from estuaries during the winter (Whitewater Bay: Tabb and Manning 1961; Aransas Bay: Copeland 1965).  The only months Silverstripe halfbeaks were absent from the Indian River Lagoon seagrass collections were December and January, as adults (to 240 mm SL) were collected during all other months (Gilmore 1988; Gilmore unpubl. data).  The smallest individuals captured within the lagoon were 25 mm SL in March while specimens below 75 mm SL were captured March through July (Gilmore 1988; Gilmore unpub data).

sections.heading: BENTHIC HABITAT
sections.content:
Habitat Type:  Eggs are benthic in seagrass meadows (F. Douglas Martin in Hardy 1978), while larvae are apparently within the water column, though in shallow water, possibly seagrass meadows. Juveniles and adults forage in groups near surface waters over seagrass meadows and adjacent to sandy beaches (Gilmore pers obs).  Often captured in surface waters at night (Hoese 1958).  Also occurs in tidal channels (Yarrow 1877) and along ocean and Gulf beaches, but is more typical of bay and estuarine waters.

Substrate:  Eggs are deposited on blades of seagrass (F. Douglas Martin in Hardy 1978).  Larvae are found principally in water column often in association with floating vegetation or debris (Gilmore pers. obs.).  Juveniles and adults occur principally in the water column and near the water's surface over sand and vegetated bottoms, such as seagrass meadows (Gilmore 1987, 1988; Robertson and Klumpp 1983; Breder and Rosen 1966).

sections.heading: Salinity
sections.content: The Silverstripe halfbeak is an euryhaline marine species which resides in estuaries within the southern portion of its range.  Northern ranging individuals (north of 28 00 N) typically spend a portion of their life history on the adjacent continental shelf (Gilmore 1972; Hardy 1978). Recorded from temperatures of 16.7-34.0 C, salinity 15.9-42.9 ppt (Roessler 1970).  Larva recorded from salinities of 0.00-12.0 ppt (Dovel 1971).  Juvenile and adult halfbeaks were present in the Indian River Lagoon seagrass meadows during all months except December and January at salinities of 17-38 ppt (25 ppt mean). Kilby (1954) has recorded the Silverstripe halfbeak from salinities as low as 7.5 ppt. in marshes of the Florida coast of the Gulf of Mexico.

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content: Reproductive Mode:  This species is gonochoristic, polygamous, oviparous, and iteroparous; eggs are fertilized externally (Hildebrand and Schroeder 1928; Breder and Rosen 1966; Hardy 1978).

sections.heading: Mating/Spawning
sections.content:
Spawning apparently occurs over shallow seagrass meadows during the spring with 2.0 mm diameter egg deposition on grass blades (Hildebrand and Schroeder 1928; F. Douglas Martin in Hardy 1978).  Larvae are free swimming at 3.0 mm TL and have no beak though the dentary begins to elongate at 11 mm TL (Hildebrand and Schroeder 1928).  Young of the year are taken in most estuaries during the spring and summer (Hildebrand and Schroeder 1928; Kilby 1955; Reid 1954;  Springer and Woodburn 1960; Tabb and Manning 1961; Roessler 1970; Subrahmanyam and Drake 1975; Gilmore 1988).  Nothing is known of spawning behavior in this species although diurnal spawning in seagrass meadows with deposition of adhesive eggs on seagrass blades has been observed in Pacific species of Hyporhamphus (Hyporhamphus sajori [Temmink and Schlegal], Inaba 1931; Breder and Rosen 1966).

Fecundity: Nothing known.

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg:  Eggs are demersal, spherical, with chorionic bristles and filaments and 1.0 mm in diameter when ripe, 1.4 mm at ovulation, 2.0 mm when fertilized (Hildebrand and Schroeder 1928; Dovel 1971; Hardy and Johnson 1974; Hardy 1978).  Eggs have long adhesive chorionic filaments which allow attachment to vegetation (Hardy 1978).  The smallest free swimming larvae was 3.0 mm in length (Hildebrand and Schroeder 1928).

Larvae: Larvae range from 3.0 to 15.8 mm SL (Hardy and Johnson 1974).  Development rate unknown.

Juvenile:  Juveniles range from 22.5 to 140 mm SL (Hardy and Johnson 1974; Hardy 1978).  Developmental rate is unknown.  Juveniles school in pelagic waters over seagrass in estuaries during warm months (Hildebrand and Schroeder 1928; Kilby 1955; Reid 1954; Springer and Woodburn 1960; Tabb and Manning 1961; Roessler 1970; Subrahmanyam and Drake 1975; Gilmore 1988).

Adults:  Female maturation occurs at 147 mm SL (Beebe and Tee-Van 1928).  Age is unknown.

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: The feeding habits of larvae are unknown. Juveniles and adults omnivores feeding mostly on planktonic crustaceans and plant materials (algae and seagrass; Randall 1968; Gilmore 1972; Subrahmanyam and Drake 1975). Adults consume crabs, copepods, amphipods, polychaetes, and plant detritus (Gilmore 1972; Subrahmanyam and Drake 1975).  Estuarine halfbeaks of Australia (Hyporhamphus melanochir) switch from diurnal herbivory to nocturnal zooplankivory (Robertson and Howard 1978; Robertson and Klumpp 1983).  This may be true of the Silverstripe halfbeak as Gilmore (unpublished data) has observed plant detritus in guts of diurnally captured specimens, and a gut packed exclusively with copepods in nocturnal specimens from Santa Rosa Sound, Florida.

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content:
Predation:  Due to its abundance in costal estuaries it is highly likely that the Silverstripe halfbeak plays an important role as prey for a variety of wetland predators.

Factors Influencing Populations:  There is some indication that Silverstripe halfbeaks depend on warm, relatively clear estuarine waters with seagrass meadows for reproduction and early development.  Therefore, loss of these water quality and seagrass decline which has taken place through much of the species range may have caused significant reductions in estuarine populations. Under natural conditions predation probably plays the most significant role in influencing population patterns.
